blocks.text: Inflation is increase in the general level of prices of Goods and Services.
Purchasing power decreases in case of inflation.
During inflation the debtor/borrower benefits more than the lender.

E.g. If you borrow 10,000, from a lender at a fixed interest during inflation, the money you repay is worth less than when you borrowed it. As when inflation occurs, the general price goods and services increases, meaning the value of money decreases. When you repay the % 10,000, the money you return has less purchasing power than when you borrowed it.
__ Real Interest Rate = Nominal Interest Rate - Inflation _ Fisher's Quantity Theory
Irving Fisher gave the "Money Illusion" concept.
Fisher's Quantity Theory explains the relationship between money supply, velocity of money, price level, and transaction.
V= Velocity of Money

T = Transaction eThe equation suggests that an increase in the money supply (M) will lead to an increase in the price level (P) assuming that the velocity of money (V) and the level of transactions (T) are constant.

The theory also implies that changes in the money supply have a direct impact on inflation, as an increase in the money supply leads to an increase in the price level, which in turn reduces the purchasing power of money.

Wholesale Price Index (WPI) eIt measures the average change in prices of goods at the wholesale level. eIt also reflects the change in prices of goods before they reach consumers.
Published by: Office of Economic Adviser (OEA) under Ministry of Commerce and Industry Base Year: 2022-23 (Previously by: 2011-12) elt is published: Monthly (14 day of each month)
Weightage Distribution in WPI
Manufactured goods (64.2%)
Primary articles (22.6%)
Fuel and power (13.15%)

Cost of a fixed basket of goods in the current year WPI = 100 x Cost of fixed basket of goods in base year Consumer Price Index (CPI) eIt measures the average change in prices of goods and services at the consumer / retail level. elt reflects the cost of living for consumers.
Released by: National Statistical Office (NSO) under Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MOSPI)
Frequency: Monthly (usually 12% day of each month)
Food and Beverages (highest 45.8%)

Producer Price Index:- Measure the average change in selling prices received by domestic producers for their output.
Perspective:— Unlike CPI (buyer's perspective), PPI looks at inflation from the seller's perspective.

Significance:— It captures price changes at the "factory gate" before taxes and distribution costs are added. elt is considered a leading indicator because cost increases here are usually passed on to consumers later.
Monetary Policy Framework Agreement (MPFA)
It was signed between Gol & RBI in Feb, 2015 It mandates the RBI to maintain price stability while keeping growth in mindset with a goal to maintain CPI Inflation at (4+2)% Core Inflation
Core inflation is a measure of inflation that excludes food and energy prices. It's calculated using the consumer price index (CPI)
Index of Industrial Production (IIP) elt is a statistical indicator that measures the growth of industrial production in a country over time.
Published by: National Statistical Organisation (NSO) under MOSPI.
Eight core industries have 40% contributions in IIP in decreasing order:

Cause: A slowdown in the economy's money supply through a tighter monetary policy.
Decrease in inflation 10% 8% 7% 5% rate over the years Deflation elt is a general decrease in price of goods and services. In deflation purchasing power increases.
Cause: Reduced money supply, reduced investment, or lower production.
Phillips Curve elt is a graph that shows the relationship between unemployment and inflation in an economy.
It is a period of high inflation and low economic growth.
It's a combination of the words "stagnation" and "inflation"
(Stagflation = Stagnation + Inflation) eWhen stagflation increases, high unemployment is a direct consequence.
Cause: When the production of goods and services in an economy slows down or declines.
Shrinkflation A situation where the price of a product remains the same but the quantity or size of the product is reduced, effectively increasing the price per unit.
Bottleneck Inflation A situation where production or supply is restricted at a particular stage of the production or distribution process, causing a slowdown and leading to shortages and price rise.

Skewflation A situation where prices of essential goods (especially food items) rise sharply while prices of non-essential goods remain stable or rise slowly, causing an uneven or skewed pattern of inflation in the economy.

Reflation A deliberate government policy to increase the level of economic activity and prices by increasing money supply, government expenditure, or reducing taxes, usually to recover from recession.
Imported Inflation Inflation that occurs when the prices of imported goods and raw materials increase, which raises the overall price level in the domestic economy.
The excess of aggregate demand over aggregate supply at full employment level, which leads to upward pressure on Prices.

Parmar Sir to students: National Sample Survey
"Dil dukha hai lekin tuta Office (NSSO) uses three toh nahi aur ummeed ka methods to measure daaman abhi chhuta to Unemployment. nahi hai".
1. Usual status approach
2. Current weekly status approach.
3. Daily status approach.
A. Usual Status (US) Approach
Reference period: Last 365 days (1 year) preceding the date of survey.
Used to identify long-term or chronic unemployment.
Usual Status has two components: 1. Principal Status (PS)
The activity in which a person spent most of the time during the last 365 days.
Determined using the majority time criterion.
2. Subsidiary Status (SS)
A person may perform additional economic activity for at least 30 days during the year apart from the principal activity.
This is known as Usual Status (PS + SS).
B. Current weekly status (CWS):
In labour force for last 1 week; If able to find work for at least 1 hour on any 1 day ~ Employed C. Current Daily Status (CDS):
It measures the intensity of unemployment
In labour force for 1 day
If work >4hrs=100% engaged
If work 1-4hrs=50% engaged
If work <1hr= unemployed
Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR): The percentage of persons in the labour force (working or available for work) in the population.
Worker Population Ratio (WPR): The percentage of employed persons in the population.
Unemployment Rate (UR): The percentage of person unemployed among the persons in the labour force.
A type of unemployment that occurs when there is a mismatch between the skills of the workforce and the skills required for available jobs.
E.g. An advancement in technology like advanced machinery can replace farmer labour.
Educated unemployment is when people with academic degrees are unable to find employment. It can also be called graduate unemployment. elt is seen in urban part of India.
E.g. An engineering graduate, who is unable to find a job in their field because they lack practical skills.
A short-term type of unemployment that occurs when people search for better job that's why it is also called Search/Voluntary unemployment.
E.g. An employee leaving a current job to move to a better one as frequently seen in urban cities.
A type of unemployment where more people are working than actually needed, meaning their removal would not affect productivity.
Eg. A family of five works on a farm in rural area that could be run by three people.
Cyclical Unemployment eA type of unemployment that occurs when the labor force is reduced due to business cycles or economic fluctuations.
When economy revives, there is an opportunity to employment (mostly seen in urban areas).

NOTE: Great Recession Significant prolonged downturn of economic activity for 2 or more consecutive quarters E.g: US Subprime Lending crisis whereas prolonged recession is termed as depression. E.g. Great depression of USA (1929-1939)
Seasonal Unemployment eA type of unemployment that occurs during specific times of the year. The employment is based on seasonal basis and is mostly seen in rural part of India.
Ex: Lights or firework sellers during Diwali.
Classical Unemployment elt is also known as real wage unemployment, it occurs when the real wage for a job is too high, which leads to more job seekers than job openings.
E.g. When workers negotiate for a minimum salary that's more than what a company can afford.
Natural unemployment refers to the lowest unemployment level a healthy economy can sustain without causing inflation.
